The Aye-aye (Daubentonia madagascariensis) is the world's largest nocturnal primate and exhibits a suite of unusual life-history traits that distinguish it from other strepsirrhines. Field studies indicate that neonates are born with a wet weight of 109 grams [Wwb = 109 grams], a relatively modest mass given the species' ultimate adult dimensions. Development proceeds slowly, with young remaining dependent on maternal milk until they undergo the dietary transition to solid food at approximately 197 days after birth [tx = approximately 197 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This protracted nursing period is energetically demanding for the mother, who must provision the offspring while also meeting her own maintenance requirements. The body mass of dependent young increases steadily during the suckling stage, and by the time of weaning, the wet weight of the juvenile typically reaches about 1535 grams [Wwx = about 1535 grams]. This value represents a substantial investment by the dam and highlights the Aye-aye's relatively altricial developmental strategy compared to many other lemurids of comparable body size.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of its nocturnal activity period and resting metabolic demands, maintained at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], sexual maturity is attained at approximately 882 days after birth [tp = approximately 882 days after birth]. This remarkably late onset of puberty for a mammal of its body mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes prolonged somatic growth and the development of a sophisticated cognitive repertoire, including the specialized percussive foraging technique for which the species is famous. The delay before reproductive activation allows the skeleton and the elongated, gracile middle finger to reach full functional capacity. Comparative data from other daubentoniids are unavailable due to the family's monotypic status, but among lemurs this age at sexual maturation is among the highest recorded relative to adult body size, a pattern that aligns with the species' extremely slow life-history pace and low intrinsic population growth rate.

Reproductive output in the Aye-aye is correspondingly low, reflecting its position at the slow end of the primate life-history continuum. For a species with a maximum adult body length of 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], the observed fecundity is surprisingly modest. Females typically produce a single offspring per birth event [N_R_i = single offspring per birth event], and the interbirth interval exceeds two years, resulting in approximately one birth event every 2.5 years [F_R_i = approximately one birth event every 2.5 years]. This constrained reproductive rate is hypothesized to be an evolutionary response to both the unpredictable spatiotemporal distribution of its primary prey, wood-boring insect larvae, and the high energetic cost of lactation in a female that must sustain herself through a prolonged dry season. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult individuals, recorded at 2278 grams [Wwi = 2278 grams], suggests that the energetic burden of gestation and lactation is considerable, further limiting the frequency with which breeding can successfully occur within a population.

Under the thermal conditions typical of captive Aye-aye colonies (36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]), gestation lasts for approximately 167 days [tg = approximately 167 days] and maximum longevity approaches 23.3 years [am = 23.3 years]. This gestation period is long relative to the species' body mass when compared with other lemurs, and it may be linked to the extensive prenatal development of the brain and the specialized dentition including the continuously growing incisors. The long gestation is followed by an even longer period of postnatal dependency before the offspring gains nutritional independence. The interval from birth to weaning accounts for a substantial fraction of the total lifespan, a pattern that underscores the substantial period of maternal investment required by this species. Available zoo records indicate that the maximum longevity under favorable captive conditions approaches 23.3 years [am = 23.3 years] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This extended maximum lifespan is consistent with the slow life-history syndrome of this primate, which exhibits delayed maturation, low fecundity, and extended interbirth intervals.

The life-history profile of the Aye-aye has profound implications for its conservation status as a vulnerable and declining species. With the slowest reproductive rate of any lemur, populations are exceptionally sensitive to adult mortality from habitat fragmentation and hunting pressure. The maximum daily reproductive rate, equivalent to approximately one offspring every 918 days under ideal captive conditions maintained at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], means that even small increases in adult mortality can drive a population toward extinction through a failure to replace losses. Conservation interventions must therefore prioritize the protection of breeding adults and the preservation of continuous forest habitat that allows for the natural dispersal of sub-adults. The species' exceptionally long life, documented at 23.3 years in captivity, provides a demographic buffer only if mortality rates of adults remain very low, a condition that is increasingly difficult to maintain across the fragmented landscapes of eastern Madagascar where remnant populations now persist.
